title: Stocks log best week since April 2025; jobs report up next
dek: Weekend edition: U.S. markets are closed today after a Black Friday half-session that capped a sharp rebound led by AI and chip stocks. Next week brings OPEC+ and Spain's election on Sunday, Jensen Huang before Congress, the ISM surveys and Friday's November jobs report, all ahead of a widely expected Fed rate hike on December 9.
quick: U.S. markets are closed for the weekend. Friday's shortened session ended with the S&P 500 up 1.6% at 7,297, the Nasdaq up 2.3% and the Dow up 592 points, or 1.2%.
For the week, the S&P 500 rose about 5.6%, the Nasdaq about 6.7% and the Dow about 5.5%. Reports call it the S&P's best week since April 2025 and the Dow's best since October 2022.
Treasury yields climbed 7 to 9 basis points Friday; the 10-year closed near 4.94% and the 2-year near 4.71%. Fed funds futures price roughly a 95% to 99% chance of a quarter-point hike on December 9.
Gold jumped about 3% to near $3,650 and silver about 8% as metals bounced off recent lows. Bitcoin is stuck near $59,000 to $60,000.
Sunday: OPEC+ meets and is expected to leave output targets unchanged, and Spain holds a snap national election.
Next week's big events: Huang's testimony to Congress (December 1 and 3), the ISM surveys, Marvell, Salesforce and Snowflake earnings, and Friday's jobs report.

blocks.head: AI rebound gives stocks their best week in more than a year and a half
blocks.what: Stocks rose across the board in Friday's half-day session, which closed at 1 p.m. ET. The S&P 500 gained 1.6% to 7,297.49, the Nasdaq Composite 2.3% to 24,129.50 and the Dow 1.2% to 50,774.94. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index jumped about 4.7%, per market wraps. For the holiday-shortened week, the S&P 500 rose about 5.6%, the Nasdaq about 6.7% and the Dow about 5.5%. The S&P 500 has climbed roughly 9% from its November 20 close, when it entered a correction (a drop of 10% or more from a peak).
blocks.why: The rally recovered much of November's AI-led selloff, but the Nasdaq and S&P 500 are still on track for monthly losses going into Monday, the last trading day of November. Holiday volume was light, which can exaggerate moves. Some analysts, including writers at CNBC, point out that sharp bounces after fast corrections have often not held historically.
blocks.watch: Whether the gains hold on Monday, when month-end portfolio rebalancing can add volatility.

blocks.head: A December Fed rate hike looks all but certain
blocks.what: Fed funds futures imply about a 95% to 99% chance of a quarter-point rate increase at the December 8 to 9 meeting, according to CME FedWatch readings cited in several reports. That would lift the target range from 3.75%-4.00% to 4.00%-4.25%. The case for a hike rests on hot data. The Commerce Department revised third-quarter GDP growth up to a 4.3% annual rate from 3.4%, and core PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred gauge, ran at 3.3% from a year earlier in October. Futures also put the odds of another hike in January near 60%, per reports. The Fed's quiet period before its meeting starts today, so officials will not comment publicly on policy next week.
blocks.why: Since a December move is already reflected in short-term yields, the open question is how many more hikes follow. That keeps pressure on the 2-year yield, the dollar and rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate, utilities and small caps.
blocks.watch: Friday's November jobs report, the last major labor reading before the meeting.

blocks.head: Nvidia faces Congress next week after a volatile month
blocks.what: Nvidia rose 0.8% Friday to $150.49 but is down roughly 26% for November, per market reports. CEO Jensen Huang, back in the job, is scheduled for a closed-door transcribed interview with three House committees on December 1. On December 3 he is due as the only witness at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on oversight of U.S. chip export controls. Lawmakers are asking whether Nvidia chips reached China in violation of export rules. Separately, reports this week said Nvidia paused AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries after a new Commerce Department licensing rule. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is scheduled to testify to the same Senate committee on December 10.
blocks.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the S&P 500 and the bellwether for the AI trade, so headlines from the hearings can move the Nasdaq, chip stocks and AI server makers. Lawmakers are also negotiating bipartisan bills that would tighten chip export rules for a December defense package, reports say.
blocks.watch: Huang's public testimony on Thursday, and any change to the hearing schedule.

blocks.head: Bond yields reverse higher, led by short maturities
blocks.what: Treasury yields rose 7 to 9 basis points across maturities in Friday's shortened bond session, retracing the safe-haven buying from before Thanksgiving. The 2-year finished near 4.71%, the 10-year near 4.94% and the 30-year near 5.33%. For the week, the 2-year rose about 7 basis points while the 10- and 30-year were roughly unchanged, so the gap between short and long yields narrowed, per a Stocktwits weekly review.
blocks.why: When short-term yields rise faster than long-term ones, markets are pricing more Fed tightening. Long-term yields near 5% keep mortgage and corporate borrowing costs high and remain a hurdle for highly valued growth stocks.
blocks.watch: Tuesday's ISM manufacturing survey and Friday's jobs report for direction.

blocks.head: Black Friday online spending beats Adobe's forecast
blocks.what: Adobe counted $9.7 billion in U.S. online spending through 6:30 p.m. ET on Black Friday, up 12.8% from a year earlier, Reuters reported. Adobe projected a full-day total of $13 billion to $13.4 billion, above its earlier $12.9 billion forecast. Adobe expects $15.1 billion on Cyber Monday. Separately, reports point to cautious shoppers: rising prices and energy costs tied to the Iran war are squeezing holiday budgets.
blocks.why: Strong online numbers favor large e-commerce players such as Amazon, while signs of budget-conscious shoppers could weigh on traditional retailers. Holiday spending data will also feed into how investors judge the consumer as the Fed raises rates.
blocks.watch: Adobe's final weekend and Cyber Monday tallies, and Kroger and Dollar General results on Thursday.

blocks.text: Asia (Friday close)

Asian markets ended the week strongly as the AI selloff eased. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 2.1% to 58,711, Hong Kong's Hang Seng gained 2.1% and the Shanghai Composite jumped 3.7%. Chipmakers led in South Korea and Japan. Tokyo's core consumer prices rose 2.9% from a year earlier in November, the fastest pace in 16 months, which added to expectations that the Bank of Japan raises rates in December. Asian markets are closed for the weekend.
Europe (Friday close)

The Stoxx 600 rose about 1.1% to near 644, Germany's DAX 0.9% and Britain's FTSE 100 0.8%. Technology shares gained about 2.3%, led by chip-equipment names such as ASML and ASM International, and miners climbed about 3.5% as copper and gold rebounded, per Reuters-based reports. The Irish Times, citing Reuters, called it the region's strongest weekly gain since mid-May, though the index is still set for a loss for November. In company news, German defense maker Rheinmetall scaled back its growth targets, and budget airline Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy, citing high fuel costs.

Spain holds a snap national election on Sunday. Recent polls show the conservative Popular Party and the far-right Vox together near a majority of seats, which would end Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's eight years in office. Spanish bonds and bank stocks are the most exposed to the result when markets reopen Monday.
Currencies

The dollar firmed Friday as U.S. yields rose. The dollar index ended near 104.0, up about 0.4% on the day and about 0.2% on the week, near its highest level since early 2025 and on track for a third straight monthly gain. The euro was flat at $1.093. The yen weakened to about 159.6 per dollar, close to the 160 level where Japan has stepped in before, so traders are watching for official warnings. The pound slipped to about $1.31, and China's yuan was steady near 6.65 per dollar.

U.S. markets are closed today. The table below shows Friday's final readings, the end of a short week that reversed much of November's damage. Growth stocks led: the Nasdaq outgained the Dow, and the Russell 2000 of smaller companies rose 1.7%, a sign that buying spread beyond the megacaps. The VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, fell about 11% to 23.8. It is still above its long-run average near 20, so investors remain more nervous than usual.

Stock futures reopen Sunday evening. On Monday, month-end rebalancing by pension funds and other big investors, plus any reaction to Sunday's OPEC+ and Spain results, could set the tone for the first full week of December.

The 2-year yield ended Friday near 4.71%, the 10-year near 4.94% and the 30-year near 5.33%. The 10-year sits about 23 basis points above the 2-year, and the 30-year about 62 basis points above it. The curve narrowed this week because the 2-year, which tracks Fed expectations most closely, rose while longer yields held steady. Long-term yields are below the roughly 5.3% peak the 10-year reached in late September and early October, but remain near their highest levels in about two decades.

The Fed has been raising rates to fight inflation that was pushed up partly by energy costs from the Iran war. Markets treat a quarter-point hike on December 9 as nearly certain, with CME FedWatch readings between about 95% and 99%. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has said a half-point move should be considered, but futures put the odds of that at under 10%, per reports. Futures also put the chance of another hike in January near 60% and in March near 30%.
Fed speakers

items: None. The Fed's pre-meeting quiet period begins today and runs through the December 9 decision, so there will be no policy comments from officials next week.
That puts more weight on the data: ISM manufacturing and JOLTS job openings (Tuesday), ISM services (Thursday) and the jobs report (Friday).

blocks.text: All 11 S&P 500 sectors rose Friday. Technology led with a gain of about 2.8%, followed by consumer discretionary (up 2.1%) and communication services (up 2.0%), the same AI- and growth-heavy groups that fell hardest in November. Materials gained 1.8% as metals prices rebounded. Defensive sectors lagged: utilities and health care each rose about 0.3% and consumer staples about 0.4%, as investors moved out of safer stocks and into the rebound.
Notable movers Friday

items: Sandisk: up about 16%, the top S&P 500 gainer, as memory-chip stocks rebounded. Micron rose about 7.6%.
XP: up about 18% after Brazil's President Lula named Bradesco chairman Luiz Carlos Trabuco as finance minister starting in January. Other Brazil-linked stocks also rose.
Newmont: up about 5.4% as gold and silver rallied, lifting mining stocks broadly.
Vertex Pharmaceuticals: down about 5% after the FDA delayed a decision on a key kidney drug.
SpaceX: up more than 4%, joining the tech rally after Elon Musk said he would expand his share donations to children's Trump Accounts.
Nvidia: up 0.8% to $150.49, lagging other chip stocks ahead of next week's congressional hearings.

blocks.text: Oil

Brent crude ended the week near $95.40 a barrel and U.S. benchmark WTI near $83.30, down about 0.4% Friday. OPEC+ meets Sunday. Reuters and Bloomberg sources say the group is expected to keep output targets unchanged into the first quarter of 2027, while the Iran war disrupts exports from Middle East members. The group is also arguing over capacity estimates: Iraq and Kazakhstan want higher ones. The meeting is the first since the United Arab Emirates left OPEC to pump more oil. Rystad Energy forecasts a global surplus of about 5 million barrels a day next year, which would put downward pressure on prices if supply disruptions ease.
Gold and silver

Gold rose about 3% to near $3,650 an ounce Friday, extending a rebound from Wednesday's low near $3,425, its weakest level in more than a year. Silver jumped nearly 8% to about $44. The WSJ reported that metals had been sold earlier in the month by investors raising cash during the stock selloff, and that easing pressure helped them recover. The metals still face headwinds from rising U.S. yields and a firm dollar, which raise the cost of holding assets that pay no interest.
Crypto

Bitcoin is trading near $59,000 to $60,000 this morning and did not join the stock rebound. It briefly fell below $59,000 on Friday after hitting a two-year low near $57,300 late Wednesday, per crypto market reports. Those reports also note eight straight days of outflows from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs and sentiment gauges in extreme-fear territory. Ether is near $1,660, down slightly on the day.

blocks.text: The week starts Monday with the final trading day of November and reactions to Sunday's OPEC+ meeting and Spanish election. On Tuesday, the ISM manufacturing survey is expected to ease from 55.5, with forecasts ranging from about 53.8 to 55.2; readings above 50 signal expansion. October JOLTS job openings come out the same day, and Huang sits for his closed-door House interview. After the close, Marvell reports. Salesforce and Snowflake report Wednesday after the close. Thursday brings Huang's public Senate testimony, the ISM services survey (forecasts around 54.6 to 54.9, versus 54.5) and results from Kroger and Canada's big banks. The week's main event is Friday's November jobs report. Economists expect about 80,000 to 90,000 jobs added, unemployment steady at 4.1% and average hourly earnings up 0.3% for the month, per consensus figures from Newsquawk, The Globe and Mail and others. A strong report would reinforce bets on further hikes after December; a weak one could pull the January odds lower.

bottom_line: Markets head into the weekend after their strongest week since early 2025, but the backdrop is still a Fed that is expected to raise rates on December 9, long-term yields near 5% and an AI trade under congressional scrutiny. Friday's jobs report is the week's biggest test of the rebound.
